name: Tallow skincare

card.summary: Rubbing rendered beef fat on the face as a moisturiser, popular online with no published trials on tallow itself.
card.note: No published safety or efficacy studies of tallow on skin; any moisturiser can cause contact dermatitis in some people.

quick.overview:
Tallow skincare means using rendered beef fat, alone or blended into balms, as a face and body moisturiser. It spread through ancestral-diet and wellness communities as part of a broader move toward traditional fats.

Supporters say tallow resembles the fats in human skin. No published trial was found testing tallow on skin, so those claims are untested.
quick.mechanism: Fats and oils applied to skin generally act as occlusives, forming a layer that slows water loss. Tallow is almost entirely fat and would be expected to do something similar, but no study has tested it, and its comedogenic or irritant potential has not been published.
quick.risks: There are no published safety studies for tallow as a skin product. Moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some users, and animal fats can go rancid or carry contaminants depending on how they are prepared.

lead: Tallow skincare is the practice of applying rendered beef fat to the skin as a moisturiser, often as a whipped balm. People use it to soften and moisturise dry skin and as a short-ingredient, 'natural' alternative to commercial creams, with some also using it on the face for a smoother, more hydrated look. Tallow is a solid fat rendered from animals, traditionally used in soap and candles, with a high triglyceride and essential fatty acid content [1][3].

Proponents online say tallow is a traditional, minimally processed moisturiser whose fatty acid profile resembles the oils of human skin. Moisturisers in general are described as products that protect and lubricate skin, largely by forming an occlusive layer that slows water loss [2].

Research on tallow itself is limited. A 2024 scoping review in Cureus screened 147 studies, included 19 comparative, basic science and animal studies, and concluded that evidence supported tallow's composition, benefits and therapeutic properties for skin while calling for more research on tallow as a human cosmetic product [4]. A 2025 cross-sectional analysis of YouTube, Instagram and TikTok posts found that claims for acne, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis were common but largely lacked cited evidence, and that most promoting posts showed financial bias [3].

chain: Rendered beef fat applied to skin
Occlusive layer slows water loss, fatty acids soften skin
angle.text: Users apply tallow balm as a moisturiser so that dry skin feels softer and looks less flaky and dull. Moisturisers generally work by slowing water loss through an occlusive film, and tallow is described by proponents as doing this with fats similar to skin's own [2][3].

infobox: Sold as cosmetics or homemade; not evaluated as a drug

paras: Tallow is rendered beef, pork or mutton fat made mostly of triglycerides. Beef tallow is about 50 percent saturated, 42 percent monounsaturated and 4 percent polyunsaturated fat, and its main fatty acids are palmitic, stearic and oleic acids [1]. Industrial tallow is the main raw material for soap [1].

Water constantly evaporates from skin, and moisturisers slow this loss as occlusives, which form a water-repelling film, or as humectants, which attract water. Petrolatum is reported to reduce water loss by about 50 to 75 percent for several hours [2]. Common ingredients include shea butter, lanolin and plant oils [2]. Daily moisturiser use can help comfort in eczema, and persistent use of products containing allergens or irritants can cause contact dermatitis [2].

Tallow gained popularity as a skincare product on social media in recent years, driven by demand for natural and sustainable beauty products [3]. The 2025 analysis of posts on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok reported that most promoting posts were from people without healthcare credentials and showed financial bias, and that most existing evidence concerns tallow's ingredients rather than tallow itself [3].
Tallow balm is discussed in ancestral-diet and wellness circles as a natural alternative to commercial moisturisers. Proponents claim it suits skin because of its fatty acid composition [3].

No published human trial testing beef tallow applied to skin was found. The 2024 Cureus scoping review addressed five questions: whether tallow's composition suits skin, its benefits, therapeutic properties, side effects and whether it is reef-safe; it found that sources were most inconsistent on side effects and that only two addressed reef safety [4]. The 2025 cross-sectional analysis is of social media claims rather than clinical outcomes [3].
